explanation:
## The program

```cpp
bool inside{ lo < x && x < hi };
bool onEdge{ x == lo || x == hi };
bool outside{ x < lo || x > hi };

std::cout << std::boolalpha;
std::cout << "inside " << inside << "\n";
std::cout << "on-edge " << onEdge << "\n";
std::cout << "outside " << outside << "\n";
```

## A condition is an ordinary value

Nothing about `lo < x && x < hi` requires an `if`. It is an
expression of type `bool`, and it can be stored, passed to a
function, returned, put in a container, or printed. Seeing that
clearly is what makes the next few hundred lines of C++ you write
shorter than they would otherwise be:

```cpp
bool ok{ n > 0 };                     // not: if (n > 0) ok = true;
return a == b;                        // not: if (a == b) return true;
while (!done) { ... }                 // not: while (done == false)
```

Each of the right-hand versions is something a beginner writes, and
each one is the same idea spelled out twice.

## Why the output needed std::boolalpha

`bool` converts to `int` as 0 or 1, and that is what the stream
prints by default:

```cpp
std::cout << (1 < 2);                     // 1
std::cout << std::boolalpha << (1 < 2);   // true
std::cout << std::noboolalpha << (1 < 2); // 1
```

It is a property of the stream, set once and in force until it is
changed — which is why one line before the three prints is enough,
and why a function that sets it has quietly changed how every other
part of the program prints a `bool`.

## lo < x < hi

This is the one to remember, because it compiles without a warning
at default settings and is wrong:

```
lo < x < hi

  is  (lo < x) < hi
  is  bool < hi
  is  0 or 1 < hi
```

With `lo = 1`, `x = 100`, `hi = 9`: `1 < 100` is `true`, `true`
becomes 1, and `1 < 9` is true. So the expression says 100 is
between 1 and 9. Python allows the chain and means the obvious
thing; C++ does not have the chain, only this accident. Write the
`&&`.

## Exactly one of three

For `lo <= hi`, the three answers partition every possible `x`:
strictly inside, on one of the ends, or beyond one of them. So a run
whose output has two `true`s or none has a bug, and that is a cheap
self-check to build into your own testing. It stops being true if
`lo > hi`, which the constraints rule out.

## What this does not check

`lo > hi`. With a reversed range the three conditions can all be
false at once, and the program says so rather than complaining. A
function taking a range from a caller would be within its rights to
assert on it.
